questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What is an 'empire'?
options: A group of countries ruled by one powerful country
questions.answer: A group of countries ruled by one powerful country
questions.hint: Think of one country controlling many others.
questions.explanation: An empire is formed when one country (the 'mother country') rules over other countries or territories (its 'colonies'). The British Empire was the largest in history.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What word describes the policy of one country building an empire by taking over other countries?
questions.answer: imperialism
questions.hint: It shares a root with 'emperor' and 'empire'.
questions.explanation: Imperialism is the policy of extending a country's power and influence by taking over other countries, often by force. The British Empire was built on imperialism.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: At its peak around 1920, what fraction of the world's land did the British Empire cover?
questions.answer: About 25%
questions.hint: Roughly a quarter of the Earth's surface.
questions.explanation: At its height in 1920 the British Empire covered about 25% of the world's land and ruled about 23% of the world's population — over 400 million people. It was the largest empire in history.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which phrase was famously used to describe the British Empire because it was so vast?
options: 'The empire on which the sun never sets'
questions.answer: 'The empire on which the sun never sets'
questions.hint: It meant the sun was always shining somewhere in the empire.
questions.explanation: Because the empire spanned every continent and time zone, the sun was always shining on some part of it. The phrase celebrated the empire's vastness.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which of these countries were part of the British Empire? (Select all that apply)
answer: India
Canada
Australia
Nigeria
questions.hint: Four were colonies; two were independent rivals.
questions.explanation: India, Canada, Australia and Nigeria were all British colonies. France was a rival imperial power. Japan was never colonised by Britain — it built its own empire.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which colony was called the 'Jewel in the Crown' of the British Empire?
questions.answer: India
questions.hint: It's a huge country in South Asia.
questions.explanation: India was called the 'Jewel in the Crown' because it was the empire's most valuable possession — providing huge wealth in tea, cotton, spices, and a vast army.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — Jewel in the Crown

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What name is given to the period when the British government directly ruled India (1858–1947)?
questions.answer: the British Raj
questions.hint: 'Raj' is the Hindi word for 'rule' or 'reign'.
questions.explanation: The British Raj was the period from 1858 (when the British Crown took over from the East India Company) until Indian independence in 1947. 'Raj' means 'rule' in Hindi.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Raj

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which British TRADING company actually ruled large parts of India before the British government took over in 1858?
questions.answer: The East India Company
questions.hint: Its name tells you which part of the world it traded with.
questions.explanation: The East India Company was a British trading company founded in 1600. Astonishingly, it ended up ruling much of India with its own private army — until the 1857 Indian Rebellion led the British government to take over directly.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which great Indian empire ruled most of India BEFORE the British arrived, and was famous for buildings like the Taj Mahal?
questions.answer: The Mughal Empire
questions.hint: Their name sounds a bit like 'Mongol' but they ruled India.
questions.explanation: The Mughal Empire (1526–1857) ruled most of the Indian subcontinent. They built incredible architecture (including the Taj Mahal) and had a sophisticated economy. Britain conquered them gradually.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Mughal India (diversity)

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why is it important to study Mughal India when studying the British Empire?
options: It reminds us that India was a rich, advanced civilisation long before British rule — the British did not bring 'civilisation' to a backward land
Mughal art was the only Indian art
questions.answer: It reminds us that India was a rich, advanced civilisation long before British rule — the British did not bring 'civilisation' to a backward land
questions.hint: Older British histories ignored Mughal achievements — why does that matter?
questions.explanation: Mughal India had vast wealth, world-class architecture, sophisticated administration and high literacy. Studying it challenges the myth that the British 'civilised' India. India was already civilised — the British just took it over.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Mughal India

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What name is given to the British tactic of setting different groups (e.g. religions, tribes, castes) against each other to keep control of a colony?
questions.answer: Divide and Rule
questions.hint: Two short words joined by 'and' — a strategy of separation.
questions.explanation: 'Divide and Rule' was a deliberate British strategy: by encouraging Hindus and Muslims (in India) or different tribes (in Africa) to mistrust each other, the British could rule a much larger population with fewer soldiers.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — Divide and Rule

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: How did the British use 'Divide and Rule' in India?
options: They encouraged religious tensions between Hindus and Muslims and treated different groups differently to prevent them uniting against British rule
They divided India into hundreds of small states
They forced everyone to speak English
questions.answer: They encouraged religious tensions between Hindus and Muslims and treated different groups differently to prevent them uniting against British rule
questions.hint: Britain played religions and groups off against each other.
questions.explanation: The British exploited and worsened religious and caste divisions in India. For example, they reserved certain government jobs for one group, gave separate electorates, and stoked Hindu-Muslim tension — making unified resistance harder.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — Divide and Rule

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was a tragic long-term consequence of Britain's 'Divide and Rule' in India?
options: When Britain left in 1947, India and Pakistan were violently partitioned along religious lines, displacing 15 million people and causing up to 2 million deaths
Hindus and Muslims became close allies
questions.answer: When Britain left in 1947, India and Pakistan were violently partitioned along religious lines, displacing 15 million people and causing up to 2 million deaths
questions.hint: Partition in 1947 — one of the largest forced migrations in human history.
questions.explanation: When Britain left in 1947, India was partitioned into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan. The hatred stoked by decades of Divide and Rule led to horrific violence — up to 2 million dead and 15 million displaced.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — Divide and Rule / Partition

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which raw materials did Britain take from its colonies? (Select all that apply)
answer: Tea from India
Cotton from India and Egypt
Sugar from the Caribbean
Rubber from Malaya
questions.hint: Four were genuine colonial resources; one is a joke.
questions.explanation: Britain extracted tea, cotton, sugar, rubber, spices, gold, diamonds, ivory and many other resources from its colonies. These raw materials were processed in British factories and sold worldwide.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Empire resources

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why was India called the 'Jewel in the Crown'?
options: It was the empire's most valuable colony — providing wealth, raw materials and the largest colonial army
All British kings were crowned there
questions.answer: It was the empire's most valuable colony — providing wealth, raw materials and the largest colonial army
questions.hint: The phrase wasn't just about beauty — it was about value.
questions.explanation: India provided enormous wealth (taxes, raw materials, market for British goods) and a huge army of Indian soldiers that Britain used to police the rest of the empire. Losing India would devastate Britain's position.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — Jewel in the Crown

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was the Indian Rebellion (or 'Mutiny') of 1857?
options: A massive uprising of Indian soldiers and civilians against East India Company rule — brutally crushed by the British
questions.answer: A massive uprising of Indian soldiers and civilians against East India Company rule — brutally crushed by the British
questions.hint: It started among 'sepoys' — Indian soldiers serving Britain.
questions.explanation: The 1857 Rebellion began with Indian soldiers (sepoys) and spread into a wider uprising against British rule. Both sides committed atrocities. Britain crushed it ruthlessly, then abolished the East India Company and brought India under direct Crown rule.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What were 'colonies'?
options: Countries or territories controlled by another (more powerful) country
questions.answer: Countries or territories controlled by another (more powerful) country
questions.hint: Britain had hundreds of these around the world.
questions.explanation: Colonies are territories ruled by a foreign (imperial) power. The people who settle in or are sent to administer colonies are called 'colonists' or 'colonialists'.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which were reasons Britain built such a large empire? (Select all that apply)
options: To get raw materials for industry
To open markets for British manufactured goods
National pride and competition with rivals (France, Spain, later Germany)
A belief that British civilisation was superior
answer: To get raw materials for industry
To open markets for British manufactured goods
National pride and competition with rivals (France, Spain, later Germany)
A belief that British civilisation was superior
questions.hint: Four real motives, one modern justification that wasn't a genuine cause.
questions.explanation: Britain built its empire for raw materials, markets, prestige, naval bases, and a belief in racial/cultural superiority. 'Spreading democracy' was sometimes claimed but rarely practised — most colonies had no democratic rights at all.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — British Empire causes

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Roughly when did the British Empire reach its largest size?
questions.answer: About 1920 (after WWI)
questions.hint: It peaked after the First World War.
questions.explanation: The British Empire reached its largest extent around 1920, when Britain gained former German and Ottoman territories as 'mandates' after WWI. Decline started after WWII.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which arguments are used to support the view that the British Empire was a 'force for good'? (Select all that apply)
options: Built railways, schools and hospitals in colonies
Spread the English language used worldwide today
Ended the slave trade and slavery in its colonies (1807/1833)
Created legal systems still used in many countries
answer: Built railways, schools and hospitals in colonies
Spread the English language used worldwide today
Ended the slave trade and slavery in its colonies (1807/1833)
Created legal systems still used in many countries
questions.hint: Four are arguments FOR; one is an argument AGAINST.
questions.explanation: Defenders point to infrastructure, language, ending slavery (after starting it!), and legal systems. Critics point to violence, theft of resources, famines, racism and the destruction of local economies. Historians genuinely debate this.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — Was the Empire a force for good?

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which arguments are used to support the view that the British Empire was NOT a force for good? (Select all that apply)
options: Famines caused by British policies (e.g. Bengal famines killed millions)
Massacres like Amritsar (1919) where troops killed hundreds of peaceful protestors
Theft of artefacts like the Koh-i-Noor diamond
answer: Famines caused by British policies (e.g. Bengal famines killed millions)
Massacres like Amritsar (1919) where troops killed hundreds of peaceful protestors
Theft of artefacts like the Koh-i-Noor diamond
Violent partition of India in 1947
questions.hint: Four serious harms; one trivial 'achievement'.
questions.explanation: Critics point to British-caused famines (Bengal 1770 killed millions; 1943 famine killed 3 million), massacres (Amritsar 1919), economic exploitation, racism, theft of art and artefacts, and the chaos of decolonisation.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — Was the Empire a force for good?

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was the Amritsar Massacre of 1919?
options: When British troops under General Dyer opened fire on a peaceful Indian crowd, killing around 400 and wounding over 1,000
An Indian attack on the British
questions.answer: When British troops under General Dyer opened fire on a peaceful Indian crowd, killing around 400 and wounding over 1,000
questions.hint: It happened at Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden in Amritsar.
questions.explanation: On 13 April 1919, General Dyer ordered troops to fire on around 20,000 unarmed Indians in a walled garden in Amritsar. At least 379 were killed (Indian estimates say over 1,000). It turned many Indians decisively against British rule.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire violence

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which famous leader used non-violent civil disobedience to campaign for Indian independence from Britain?
questions.answer: Mahatma Gandhi
questions.hint: His followers called him 'Mahatma' — meaning 'great soul'.
questions.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi led the Indian independence movement using non-violent civil disobedience — boycotts, strikes, marches (like the Salt March of 1930). India gained independence in 1947 partly because of his campaigns.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire / India

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: In which year did India gain independence from Britain?
questions.hint: Just after the Second World War.
questions.explanation: India and Pakistan gained independence from Britain on 15 August 1947, after decades of campaigning by Gandhi, Nehru, Jinnah and millions of others.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What word describes the process of colonies gaining their independence from an empire?
questions.answer: decolonisation
questions.hint: Add 'de-' to the start of a word meaning 'becoming a colony'.
questions.explanation: Decolonisation is the process by which colonies gain independence. Most British colonies became independent between 1947 (India) and the 1960s–70s, though Hong Kong wasn't returned until 1997.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire legacy

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Put these events in the history of the British Empire in chronological order.
options: Indian Rebellion / start of British Raj
answer: Founding of Jamestown colony
Indian Rebellion / start of British Raj
Amritsar Massacre
Indian independence
questions.hint: Jamestown 1607, Indian Rebellion 1857, Amritsar 1919, Indian independence 1947.
questions.explanation: Jamestown (1607), Indian Rebellion / British Raj begins (1857–58), Amritsar Massacre (1919), Indian Independence (1947).
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which racist idea was used in the 19th century to justify European empires?
options: The idea that white Europeans had a duty to 'civilise' non-white peoples — sometimes called 'the white man's burden'
The belief in equality between races
The idea that all empires were bad
questions.answer: The idea that white Europeans had a duty to 'civilise' non-white peoples — sometimes called 'the white man's burden'
questions.hint: The phrase came from a 1899 poem by Rudyard Kipling.
questions.explanation: Imperialists justified empire with racist 'civilising mission' ideas — claiming non-European peoples were inferior and needed European rule. Rudyard Kipling's 1899 poem 'The White Man's Burden' summed up this thinking. It was used to excuse violent conquest.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — British Empire

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which of these are LEGACIES of the British Empire we can still see today? (Select all that apply)
options: English is one of the most widely spoken languages in the world
Cricket is popular in many former colonies
Borders drawn by Britain still cause tensions (e.g. India/Pakistan, Middle East)
answer: English is one of the most widely spoken languages in the world
Cricket is popular in many former colonies
Borders drawn by Britain still cause tensions (e.g. India/Pakistan, Middle East)
The Commonwealth of Nations
questions.hint: Britain has no colonies today, but the empire's effects continue.
questions.explanation: Modern legacies include English as a global language, cricket, borders the British drew, the Commonwealth, multicultural Britain, and unresolved debates about reparations and stolen artefacts.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire legacy

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What name is given to the modern association of former British colonies that now cooperate voluntarily?
questions.answer: the Commonwealth
questions.hint: It's a 'wealth' that countries hold in 'common'.
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth of Nations is a voluntary association of 56 mostly-former British colonies. The British monarch is its symbolic head, but members are independent and equal.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire legacy

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What name is given to the rapid colonisation of Africa by European powers in the late 1800s?
questions.answer: Scramble for Africa
questions.hint: European countries 'scrambled' to claim African land.
questions.explanation: The Scramble for Africa (c.1881–1914) was when European powers — especially Britain, France, Germany and Belgium — competed to colonise Africa. The 1884 Berlin Conference divided the continent on a map with no Africans present.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — British Empire / Africa

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was the impact of European powers drawing African borders at the 1884 Berlin Conference?
options: Borders were drawn with no regard for African languages, tribes or kingdoms — splitting some peoples and forcing others to share a country, causing conflicts that continue today
Africans were happy with the borders
Borders followed all existing tribal boundaries
It had no impact on Africa
questions.answer: Borders were drawn with no regard for African languages, tribes or kingdoms — splitting some peoples and forcing others to share a country, causing conflicts that continue today
questions.hint: Modern African conflicts often trace back to colonial-era borders.
questions.explanation: European leaders drew straight lines across Africa to divide it among themselves, ignoring centuries-old kingdoms, tribes and languages. Many modern African conflicts (e.g. Rwanda, Sudan, Nigeria) can be traced to these arbitrary colonial borders.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — British Empire / Africa

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why is it important to study the perspectives of colonised people (Indians, Africans, indigenous peoples) and not just the British view of empire?
options: History looks very different from below — colonised peoples experienced violence, theft and loss of freedom that British histories often hide
questions.answer: History looks very different from below — colonised peoples experienced violence, theft and loss of freedom that British histories often hide
questions.hint: Whose history gets told changes what we 'know'.
questions.explanation: British school textbooks once told a glorious story of empire. But the same events looked very different to those colonised — famine, massacre, loss of land. Studying multiple perspectives gives us a fuller, fairer history.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire perspectives

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What is meant by the term 'colonialism'?
options: A policy of taking control of another country, exploiting it economically, and often settling colonists there
questions.answer: A policy of taking control of another country, exploiting it economically, and often settling colonists there
questions.hint: Closely related to 'imperialism' but specifically about colonies.
questions.explanation: Colonialism is the practice of one country controlling another country (or its people), usually for economic gain. It often involves sending settlers, taking land, and imposing the coloniser's language, religion or laws.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why is the Koh-i-Noor diamond controversial today?
options: It was taken from a 10-year-old Maharaja under duress in 1849 and now sits in a British Crown — India, Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran have all asked for it back
It is too small to wear
questions.answer: It was taken from a 10-year-old Maharaja under duress in 1849 and now sits in a British Crown — India, Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran have all asked for it back
questions.hint: It's a symbol of debates about returning looted artefacts.
questions.explanation: The Koh-i-Noor ('Mountain of Light') diamond was taken from Maharaja Duleep Singh in 1849. It's now in the British Crown Jewels. Multiple countries have demanded its return — part of wider debates about restitution of colonial loot.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire legacy

further_learning.title: KS3 History Units – Oak National Academy
KS3 History – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: When historians ask 'Was the British Empire a force for good?', why is there no single right answer?
options: Because it depends on whose experience you measure, which time period you look at, and which costs and benefits you count — historical interpretations are always debated
Because no one cares about empires
Because the empire had only positive effects
Because the empire had only negative effects
questions.answer: Because it depends on whose experience you measure, which time period you look at, and which costs and benefits you count — historical interpretations are always debated
questions.hint: Historical questions usually have more than one valid answer.
questions.explanation: Different historians weigh evidence differently. A railway in India was good for British exports but built using cheap Indian labour. Ending the slave trade was good but Britain started it. Honest historians take multiple perspectives seriously.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — British Empire interpretations
